newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Euro to boost pressure on financial industry-BIS.
newsitem.headline: Euro to boost pressure on financial industry-BIS.

text.p: A single European currency is likely to increase the competitive pressure on Europe's banks and intensify the need to restructure the financial industry, economists at the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) said.

The probable introduction of the euro is likely to become a catalyst for change that goes well beyond the need to absorb the direct cost of transition, BIS economic advisor William White and economist Robert McCauley wrote in BIS working paper: The Euro and European Financial Markets.
Initially, the euro is likely to stimulate growth of a much larger and more liquid securities market and banks could quickly find themselves in a vicious circle.
Deeper and more liquid bond markets puts traditional bank lending at a disadvantage and erodes their profit margins.
This could trigger lower credit ratings and encourage bank customers to go directly to financial markets, adding further competitive pressure, the economists said.

Although asset managers would be attracted to shift funds into an increasingly deep and liquid euro market, the economists cautioned this will not automatically lead to a strong euro as debtors will also be encouraged to issue in euro assets.

"One should not attempt to calculate the effects of the greater attraction of the euro for official and private asset managers without considering that it might hold a similar attraction for debt managers," the report said.

Banks are likely to respond to the increasingly competitive environment in Europe in various ways, either by cost cutting, taking on more risks, turning to new lines of business or through consolidation.
However, a consolidation of the industry through mergers and acquisitions will challenge public policy in Europe, where there is still strong resistance to closing down unprofitable banks.

"Should the current resistance of national governments to closures also be maintained, ongoing competition from non-viable banks could continue to threaten the prospects of other banks and the health of the financial system more broadly," it said.
Europe's handling of its banking problems will not only have repercussions on other financial markets, but international cooperation in regulation and supervision might also change.
"...the bargaining dynamics of achieving global agreements could well be different in the future should Europe increasingly speak with a single voice," the economists said.
The report argues that the introduction of the euro comes at a time when Europe's banks are already grappling with global challenges and quickening technological innovation.

"The direct costs associated with the introduction of a single currency, and the associated increase in competition in the context of EMU, will put further pressure on bank profits and encourage adjustment of various sorts," the paper said.
Introduction of the euro will increase banks' costs during and after the transition period. During the transition computer systems must be altered, customers advised and staff trained.
After the introduction, banks will have extra note-handling costs and lose revenue from foreign exchange trading.
Salomon Brothers, for example, has estimated that net revenue from foreign exchange trading could fall by 10 percent.
While countries are expected to gain from the Economic and Monetary Union (EMU), it will be a mixed blessing for banks.
"Banks will share in the benefits of faster growth, but lower inflation could well lead to a reduction in interest rate spreads," the economist said.
Monetary union is expected to increase competition in Europe's bond markets, currently segmented by currencies.
But as currency has been more of a factor influencing competition than relations between customers and underwriters, a single currency will erode some of banks' past advantages.
This means the advantage German banks have had in the euro-mark market will not carry over to the euro capital market.
The economists also address the issue of whether the euro automatically will be a strong currency.
The greater depth of the euro bond market is likely to be a more attractive place for asset managers to invest.
Although the euro should benefit from portfolio allocations at the expense of the dollar, the economist said this does not necessarily mean the euro will be a strong currency.
Debtors, both companies and governments, outside Europe could also find the euro an attractive market in which to issue.
"Thus a larger, broader and deeper and more liquid bond market in Europe does not necessarily imply that the value of the euro will benefit from net portfolio shifts," it said.
